To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

QSOs at redshift z ∼ 1.4 are biased tracers of the underlying matter distribution, and the bias does not depend strongly upon luminosity; the mass of the underlying dark matter halo does not evolve strongly over the redshift range z∼ 2-1; the black hole mass of QSOs is similar over a wide range in luminosity; and the Eddington efficiency of QSOs does not depend strongly with black hole mass.

(1) the clustering signal of QSOs at z ∼ 1.4 can be used to measure cosmological parameters; (2) QSOs at fixed redshift do not inhabit haloes of different masses and (3) QSOs of similar luminosity may inhabit haloes of similar black hole masses, and hence may have similar Eddington efficiencies.

the clustering of QSOs is consistent with the expectation that they inhabit dark matter haloes of similar masses, and that the QSOs of the 2SLAQ sample are not significantly more luminous than those of the 2dFRS sample.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
our data favour models which predict that the mass of the host haloes does not evolve strongly and does not depend strongly with luminosity.
the data are more consistent, although not strongly so, with a 'constant halo mass' scenario, where all QSOs reside in dark matter haloes of similar masses, than with the 'high peaks' scenario.
the data are consistent with QSOs of similar mass being found in haloes of a similar mass, but this conclusion is dependent on the assumptions made in the modelling.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the QSO bias is independent of luminosity and evolves little with redshift.
the clustering of z ∼ 1.4 QSOs is consistent with a bias of b ∼ 1 and that the QSOs are hosted by dark matter haloes of similar masses, ∼ 3 × 1011 h−1 M ⊙.
QSOs are biased tracers of the underlying dark matter distribution and that the bias does not depend strongly upon QSO luminosity.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the clustering of QSOs is not a strong function of luminosity, and this is consistent with the hypothesis that black holes in QSOs are not strongly dependent on halo mass.
QSO clustering can be used to constrain the cosmological model, and that the luminosity function of the QSO population may be a more powerful probe of cosmology than previously thought.
QSO clustering is not a strong probe of the cosmological density of the Universe.
